newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to decide on further cuts in November.
newsitem.headline: Germany to decide on further cuts in November.

text.p: The German government said on Monday it would wait until November to see how the economy and tax revenues are doing before deciding whether to make further savings on top of its current austerity package.

A finance ministry spokeswoman played down weekend comments by Health Minister Horst Seehofer, who announced further cuts on top of the government's current 70 billion mark ($46.27 billion) saving plan.

The spokeswoman said that economic forecasts due in late October and a November tax revenue estimate must be reviewed before agreeing on further action. "Only then can we decide what we have to do," she said.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative coalition won tight parliamentary votes last Friday on cuts in sick pay, pension and health reforms and a reduction in job protection, making sure that most of its savings package is now assured.

But Seehofer told Bild am Sonntag newspaper the decisions taken so far amounted to no more than a "minimal programme." He said there had to more savings in the budget, in taxes and in health and pension insurance.

Adding to the impression that Seehofer had jumped the gun on the austerity debate, a spokesman for the social affairs ministry also said there were no concrete plans for saving yet -- nor had they even been discussed.

Bonn's crunch savings plan is aimed at bringing down the budget deficit to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product next year from an expected four percent this year. That would bring Germany within the Maastricht Treaty's three percent deficit limit on qualifying for European monetary union in 1999.

Economists are sceptical that targets can be met and Finance Minister Theo Waigel repeated his position on Monday that further savings would be needed before the final reading of his 1997 budget in parliament in November.
In an apparent reference to likely shortfalls in funding the state jobless benefits scheme, Waigel said savings would come where spending was overshooting. He did not give details.

News magazine Der Spiegel reported that Bonn planned to save six to seven billion marks through cuts in unemployment benefit, reductions in job creation schemes in eastern Germany and rules requiring the unemployed to accept low-paid jobs.

Economists say years more belt-tightening will be needed to overcome the lingering impact of reunification. High unemployment, a slide in living standards to the European average and an ageing population all threaten state finances.
Norbert Walter, chief economist of Deutsche Bank, said that the government austerity package marked the starting point of a long period of saving in Germany.
"For the next 10 to 15 years I see absolutely no chance of the process of permanent savings stopping," Walter told Saarland radio.
Walter said one target should be an increase in personal payments to health insurance policies to balance health funds' budgets, otherwise the system could become unsustainable.
Economists at Salomon Brothers said the measures passed last week would have only a slight impact on jobs and growth.
"More aggressive changes probably are needed to sustain long-term potential economic growth," they wrote in a report.
